newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong stocks up sharply on back of Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong stocks up sharply on back of Wall Street.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks closed markedly higher on Monday, buoyed by Wall Street's rebound, but industrial strife in Seoul slashed more than 2.50 percent off South Korean shares.
Most Asian markets gained, with Tokyo adding half a percent on its first trading day of the year, Singapore rising one percent and Jakarta gaining 1.20 percent.

Brokers said Hong Kong's key Hang Seng index, which climbed 1.67 percent, was boosted by positive sentiment in the property and finance sectors and underpinned by Wall Street's 100-point rise on Friday..
"The market's momentum derives in large part from Wall Street's 100-point rebound...," said Anthony Mak, sales director at Vickers Ballas.
The Hang Seng Index jumped 221.14 points to 13,443.93, the high for the day. Turnover was a robust HK$11.13 billion (US$1.44 billion), slightly up on Friday's HK$11.09 billion.
The Dow rose 101.60 points, roughly 1.6 percent, to 6,544.09 on Friday as investors became more confident the U.S. economy would grow at a moderate rate.
Tokyo stocks closed higher as selective buying of shares in blue-chip companies helped a market still suffering from an uncertain outlook for the economy, dealers said.
They also said that the market had been depressed earlier in the morning after the dollar hit a near 46-month high of 117.00 yen, but losses were limited.
The benchmark Nikkei 225 average finished the half-day session up 84.65 points or 0.44 percent at 19,446.00.

"While the market overall has been anxious about the future of the economy, the trend of selective buying (in blue-chip issues) intensified," said Tadahiro Kamogawa, a senior analyst at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.
The Japanese stock market has been dragged down by lingering worries over Japan's economic growth in early 1997 and a lack of solid government proposals to shore up the economy.
Jakarta shares ended up but off earlier highs as some investors took profits in the late afternoon session.
The Jakarta Composite Index rose 7.76 points, or 1.20 percent, to close at 653.96 points after touching a high of 654.13 points in morning session.
Singapore shares gained one percent, helped by institutional demand for blue chip stocks after a bullish run in Wall Street.
The Straits Times Industrials Index rose 21.64 points or 0.97 percent to end at the session's high of 2,245.72.
Taiwan share prices rebounded from Saturday's 1.64 percent fall as political uncertainties appeared to ease, brokers said.
The index ended 24.40 points or 0.36 percent higher at 6,844.75, off a 6,865.07 high.

Analysts said there were still worries following the shock New Year's Eve resignation of Taiwan's governor, who has rejected a central government plan to dismantle his largely redundant provincical administration.
Seoul stocks fell 2.57 percent as spreading labour unrest undermined sentiment, brokers said.
"This is having a very big impact on the market," said broker Jay Kwon of Hanhwa Securities.
The composite stock index fell 16.54 points to provisionally close at 626.87. Declining shares eclipsed advancers, 763 to 70, while only 17.6 million shares changed hands.

Labour strikes flared again with renewed militancy on Monday after prosecutors summoned top union leaders for questioning. Almost 150,000 workers walked out, calling for a repeal of a controversial new labour bill.
February Brent crude futures were firmer, last trading at $24.25 a barrel on SIMEX, was up 13 cents from London's Friday settlement.
Hong Kong gold ended at US$360.50/361.00 an ounce against New York's US$360.75/361.25 close on Friday.
At 1103 GMT the dollar was trading at 115.85/5.95 yen and 1.5662/67 marks.
